title: AI Engineering at Jane Street - John Crepezzi
talk_summary: John Crepezzi describes Jane Street's AI dev-tools stack: a fine-tuned OCaml diff model trained on workspace snapshots, an RL/eval loop built on a pre-warmed build service, and a sidecar 'AID' service that centralizes prompt/context construction so thin editor plugins share one implementation. The transferable core is the architecture discipline (one sidecar, pluggable models/context, A/B testing, verifiable eval loop), not the fine-tuning itself.

takeaways.technique: Pre-warmed build service as shared RL/eval harness
takeaways.what_they_do: They keep a build pre-warmed at a green revision; workers apply model-produced diffs all day and report red/green plus the error, and the same service doubles as evaluation by holding out RL data.
takeaways.evidence_quote: first we pre-warm a build it sits at a a revision and is green and then we have these workers that all day just take diffs from the model

takeaways.what_they_do: They define 'good code' operationally (parses, typechecks, compiles, passes tests) and score model output against those checks rather than human judgment, and they hold out data to evaluate.

A single 'AID' sidecar on each dev machine owns prompt construction, context building, build-status lookup, and tool exposure; editor plugins are thin, and restarting AID rolls out changes everywhere.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Aid handles all of the uh ability to construct prompts and to construct context ... we can just restart the Aid Service on all of the boxes

takeaways.technique: A/B test models on acceptance rate
takeaways.what_they_do: AID lets them split traffic, e.g. 50% of users on one model and 50% on another, then compare acceptance rates to pick the winner.
takeaways.evidence_quote: send 50% of the company to one model and 50% to another and then determine which one gets the higher acceptance rate

takeaways.technique: Train/eval on the exact test-time shape
takeaways.what_they_do: They learned that dumping repo code doesn't work; training examples must match the inference shape (context + human-style prompt + diff), so they mined snapshots and generated short human-like descriptions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you have to have the model see a bunch of examples that are in the shape of the type of question that you want to ask the model

takeaways.technique: Snapshot build-status transitions as defect signal
takeaways.what_they_do: They snapshot workstations every ~20s with build status; green→red→green marks an isolated change and red→green captures an error plus its fix, usable as recovery training data.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you have a green to Red to Green that often corresponds to a place where a developer has made an isolated change
